title: With Due Respect (Vol. 7) -- Ch. 1: Sanctity of Life and of Marriage
keywords: Sanctity of Life and of Marriage
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7) -- CJP's October 3, 2010 Inquirer column on the 'sanctity of life and... of marriage,' the issues uniting the Catholic hierarchy against the Reproductive Health Bill and the divorce bill and making the Church 'extra sensitive' to President Aquino's pronouncements

The theology and law of life -- Humanae Vitae's condemnation of abortion and artificial contraception, and how the 1987 Constitution 'settled' the beginning-of-life debate by protecting the unborn 'from conception,' so the live dispute is now the Church's bar on artificial means of preventing the egg-sperm union

The doctrine of marital indissolubility -- the Civil and Family Codes' 'inviolable social institution' against the Church's recognition of nullity for 'psychological incapacity' that is grave, incurable and antecedent (Canon 1095, adopted as Article 36)

The jurisprudential arc CJP himself shaped -- from Santos v. CA and his own Republic v. Molina (eight guidelines) through a 'more liberal' drift and back to Suazo v. Suazo's clarification -- and why Rep. Ilagan's divorce bill, by making psychological incapacity need not be 'antecedent,' is 'theologically untenable'
sub_topics: The uniting issues: if anything unites 'the hierarchical Church,' it is 'the sanctity of life and the sanctity of marriage, which together complement the sanctity of the family' -- hence the Church's passionate opposition to the Reproductive Health Bill and the divorce bill, and its sensitivity to P-Noy

Theology of life: the 'basic Catholic theology' is Humanae Vitae (Paul VI, 1968), 'condemning abortion and prohibiting artificial contraception,' which Benedict XVI on its 40th anniversary defended as still true -- 'What was true yesterday is still true today'

The constitutional settlement: the 1987 Constitution 'outlaws abortion,' protecting 'the life of the mother and the life of the unborn from conception,' and the Penal Code long criminalized infanticide and abortion -- so, while other countries still debate when life begins, ours fixed it 'from conception' (fertilization)

The live frontier: the 'burning issue' is no longer the start of life but the Church's bar on 'any artificial means' of stopping the union of egg and sperm -- condoms, IUDs, diaphragms, ligation, vasectomy and 'pills'

Marital indissolubility: on 'what God has joined together, let no man put asunder' rests the dogma that 'no human institution, including the state, can dissolve a valid marriage,' echoed by the Civil and 1988 Family Codes' 'permanent union' and 'inviolable social institution'

Psychological incapacity: yet the Church recognizes nullity where a partner suffered 'psychological incapacity' at the marriage's inception -- Canon 1095's bar on those 'unable to assume the essential obligations,' which must be 'grave,' 'incurable' and 'antecedent' -- substantially adopted as Article 36 of the Family Code

The jurisprudence: 'the early Supreme Court decisions' -- Santos v. CA (1995, per Vitug) and CJP's own Republic v. Molina (1997, with its 'eight guidelines') -- 'closely hued to the three Church requirements,' but 'later jurisprudence... became more liberal,' until Suazo v. Suazo (2010, per Brion) clarified that Santos and Molina 'have not been abandoned and are still good case law'

The divorce-bill objection: Rep. Luzviminda Ilagan's bill proposes 'psychological incapacity' (with 'de facto' five-year separation, irreconcilable differences) as a divorce ground, but is 'theologically untenable' in proposing that the incapacity 'need not be antecedent' -- that it may arise after the rite -- thereby 'infringing [marriage's] inviolability'; CJP hopes P-Noy and the Church can avoid 'a grisly confrontation,' echoing Benedict XVI's call for 'ongoing dialogue' between secular reason and religious belief

stances.claim: On the beginning of life, our Constitution 'settled that issue' by protecting the unborn 'from conception,' so unlike countries still debating it, the Philippine question has shifted to the Church's bar on artificial means of preventing the egg-sperm union.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-settlement framing: distinguishing the Philippine debate from the global one

stances.claim: Psychological incapacity voiding a marriage must be 'grave, incurable, and antecedent,' as Canon 1095 and Article 36 require and as Santos and his own Molina held -- doctrine that 'later jurisprudence' loosened but Suazo v. Suazo confirmed is 'still good case law.'
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrine-defense by his own authorship: tracing and reaffirming the Molina standard

stances.claim: Rep. Ilagan's divorce bill is 'theologically untenable' in letting psychological incapacity arise after the wedding rather than be 'antecedent,' thereby 'infringing [marriage's] inviolability' -- though P-Noy and the Church should pursue 'ongoing dialogue,' not 'a grisly confrontation.'
stances.rhetorical_move: targeted critique with an irenic close: faulting the bill yet urging dialogue

notable_anecdotes: Three theories of life's start: CJP contrasts the global debate (egg-sperm union? viability? the umbilical cut?) with the Constitution's settled answer, 'from conception.'
His own Molina: he notes that Republic v. Molina, which he 'penned,' set the 'eight guidelines' for psychological incapacity -- and that Suazo confirmed it remains good law.
The 'antecedent' flaw: he singles out the divorce bill's proposal that psychological incapacity 'need not be antecedent' as the theologically fatal defect.
Benedict at Westminster: he closes with Benedict XVI's call before the British Parliament for 'ongoing dialogue' between secular reason and religious belief.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 7), CJP's October 3, 2010 Inquirer column, treats 'the sanctity of life and... of marriage' -- the issues uniting the Catholic hierarchy against the Reproductive Health Bill and the divorce bill, and making it 'extra sensitive' to President Aquino's pronouncements. On life, the 'basic Catholic theology' is Humanae Vitae (Paul VI, 1968), 'condemning abortion and prohibiting artificial contraception,' which Benedict XVI defended decades later: 'What was true yesterday is still true today.' The 1987 Constitution 'outlaws abortion,' protecting the unborn 'from conception,' so unlike countries still debating when life begins, the live Philippine dispute is the Church's bar on artificial means of preventing the egg-sperm union (condoms, IUDs, ligation, 'pills'). On marriage, the dogma that 'what God has joined together, let no man put asunder' makes it an 'inviolable social institution' that 'no human institution, including the state, can dissolve' -- yet the Church recognizes nullity for 'psychological incapacity' that is 'grave,' 'incurable' and 'antecedent' (Canon 1095, adopted as Article 36 of the Family Code). CJP traces the jurisprudence he helped shape: Santos v. CA (1995) and his own Republic v. Molina (1997, the 'eight guidelines') 'closely hued to the three Church requirements,' a 'more liberal' drift followed, and Suazo v. Suazo (2010) clarified that Santos and Molina remain 'good case law.' He faults Rep. Luzviminda Ilagan's divorce bill as 'theologically untenable' for letting psychological incapacity arise after the wedding rather than be 'antecedent,' thus 'infringing inviolability' -- but hopes P-Noy and the Church can avoid 'a grisly confrontation,' echoing Benedict XVI's Westminster call for 'ongoing dialogue' between secular reason and religious belief.
